subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
passage: In the Saturday sign class at the community centre, Tanuja held her hand flat near her chest, palm facing herself. "Now watch," said their teacher, and turned the palm outward, the same shape, the same movement. "Same hand. Different word." Nikita blinked. She'd assumed signs were like waving, loose and free, so who would care about the palm? "It's like vowels," the teacher signed and said aloud. "Change 'cat' to 'cot' and it's another word." Nikita practised in front of the window, palm in, palm out, carefully. When she got it wrong, the teacher gently corrected her hand. Nikita thought, this is a real language, with grammar, and I have to respect it. Tanuja gave her a thumbs-up.

qa.q: Where did the sign class meet?
qa.a: The sign class met at the community centre.

qa.q: Why did Nikita blink when the teacher turned the palm outward?
qa.a: She was surprised because she had assumed signs were loose gestures where palm direction would not matter. She then understood it changes the word.

qa.q: What could Nikita do to learn signs properly?
qa.a: Practise palm direction and handshape carefully and accept corrections, treating signing as a language with rules.

qa.q: How might a deaf signer feel if a hearing learner treated signs as loose gestures?
qa.a: They might feel disrespected, because their language has grammar and precision.

grounding: Palm direction changes a sign's meaning like a vowel changes a word, and hearing learners must respect that grammar.

subtype: Hand orientation and palm direction in signs [Interpreting]
passage:
"Watch my hand," said Gargi. "Palm toward me, then palm away. Same shape, different meaning."
"They look the same to me," said Harsha, squinting.
"How the palm faces and how the hand is aimed are part of the word, like a vowel. Change it, and it means something else."
"So I can't just wave my hand around?"
"Not if you want to be understood. Try again. Slowly."
Harsha tried, palm in, then out. Gargi signed, 'Yes, that one,' and laughed. "It's a proper language, not gestures. My cousin says people get this wrong all the time."
"Then I'd better get it right," said Harsha.

qa.q: What does Gargi say is part of the word?
qa.a: Gargi says how the palm faces and how the hand is aimed are part of the word.

qa.q: Why did Harsha squint and ask about just waving a hand around?
qa.a: Harsha believed signs were loose gestures and struggled to see the difference. The question shows Harsha had not yet understood the grammar.

qa.q: What could Harsha do to improve?
qa.a: Practise slowly with palm direction, accept Gargi's feedback and treat signing as a real language.

qa.q: How might Gargi's cousin feel when people treat signs as gestures?
qa.a: They may feel frustrated or disrespected, because their language is being ignored. 🙂

grounding: Palm direction and hand orientation carry meaning in signed languages, like vowels.
